implementation_notes: In Ruby the pattern is normally delivered by fixture tooling: factory_bot declares a factory whose attributes are the valid defaults (factory :user do email { "ada@example.com" } end) and build(:user, email: "bad@example.com") then starts from those defaults and applies only the overrides, which is the builder's defaults and chainable withX() step collapsed into one call; traits cover named variations, associations build nested graphs and build_stubbed keeps the result unsaved. Choose it whenever factories are already the suite's fixture layer, and keep create for the tests that genuinely need persistence.
pitfalls: create persists and runs callbacks, so a test that only needs an object suddenly depends on the database and on model hooks; default to build or build_stubbed.
Factory attributes can drift from the model's own validation and constructor, letting tests pass with data the domain forbids.
A factory that grows a trait per variation recreates the object mother's bloat; prefer traits for named cases plus per-call overrides.

variants.name: Hand-written keyword-argument factory method
variants.idiom_name: def a_user(email: "ada@example.com", **overrides) returning a valid PORO
variants.implementation_notes: Without fixture tooling, Ruby's keyword arguments carry the pattern: define def a_user(email: "ada@example.com", age: 30, **overrides) returning User.new(...), so a test names only the fields it asserts and a typo raises ArgumentError instead of being silently ignored. Deriving a similar object is user.dup followed by attribute writers or an explicit with_email helper, because Ruby has no copy-with syntax; keep the factory in test/support and prefer this variant for plain Minitest suites over POROs without ORM callbacks.
variants.code_sketch:
module TestData
  def a_user(email: "ada@example.com", age: 30, **overrides)
    User.new(email: email, age: age, **overrides)
  end
end

user = a_user(email: "bad@example.com")   # only the asserted field
pitfalls: **overrides accepts any keyword at the end, so a misspelled field is silently absorbed (or raises only when the constructor rejects it); keep the fields a test is likely to vary as explicit keywords.
dup is a shallow copy: instance-variable objects are shared, and models with callbacks or save-time validation still differ from instances built through the factory.
